analysis: Culture and public memory combines modern and empire history, ancient material culture, Indigenous public history, museum curation and documentary practice. Renaissance Italy and Writing Art’s Histories support visual interpretation through description-only evidence.

Politics and conflict builds historical interpretation of empire and warfare, then comparative politics, conflict studies, international law and EU institutions. General rhetoric and qualitative methods serve as transferable skills.

Economy and society adds macroeconomic policy, public economics, causal and predictive analysis and social theory to historical work. Behavioral Economics moves to an offered autumn after statistics. Public Policy Analysis replaces less relevant organisation psychology and supplies a concrete case on sugar policy.

Plausible partial connections include Modern History with the Long 20th Century, Ways of War with comparative political and military history, Renaissance Italy with one segment of the early modern survey, and World Archaeology with ancient material culture. Art historiography is narrower than general historiography. Academic rhetoric and quantitative methods do not reproduce historical source seminars. The American Century research paper is not the required Groningen thesis. Preserve the historical sequence limits and revisit alignment only against a cohort-correct comparator.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
